starting-from-requirements-constraints.explain:
## What it is

Every AI design starts by **pinning down what the system must do and what limits it lives under**, before naming a model or a vector database. Functional requirements: users, task (answer, extract, generate, act), input and output shape, what counts as correct. Non-functional: latency (interactive under ~2 s to first token versus batch overnight), volume and peak, cost ceiling per request, data sensitivity and residency, knowledge freshness, and how costly a wrong answer is.

Turn vague goals into **measurable acceptance criteria**: 'at least 90% judged correct on a 200-case set; p95 under 3 s; under $0.01 per successful ticket'. Those numbers later choose the model, the architecture, and the eval set. Skipping this is how teams pick an agent framework first and discover the latency budget or the DPA rules it out.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviews explicitly score the first minutes: clarifying questions. On the job, this is the difference between a design and a shopping list. A PM who says 'add an AI assistant' has not given you a problem yet.

## How it works + one small example

Ask, write numbers, refuse to draw boxes until you have them.

Example. 'Summarise support tickets' at 50k/day and $0.002 each points to a small model and batch. 'Answer refund questions in chat' at 2 s p95 with legal risk points to retrieval, citations, and escalation. A design with a large model and five sequential calls for autocomplete missed the latency requirement — the architecture was illegal before it was drawn.

## Failure modes

1. **Framework first.** The graph looks modern and cannot meet p95.

2. **No cost-of-error.** You treat a typo and a wrong medical dose the same.

3. **Average latency** as the requirement.

4. **Forgetting privacy** until the vendor questionnaire.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I start from users, task, quality bar, p95, volume, cost, and data constraints, and I write measurable acceptance criteria before I name a model. Architecture is a consequence of those numbers, not the other way around.

## A concrete walk-through

You spend twelve minutes asking questions. The PM wants a copilot; legal wants no health data leaving the region; p95 must be 3 s. You write three numbers on the board and only then sketch retrieve-and-generate. The agent framework stays in the parking lot.

## What I would measure

Design docs with numeric acceptance criteria; interviews where you asked before drawing; features that shipped without a p95 or a cost-of-error.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on Every AI design starts by **pinning down what the system must do and what limits is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Requirements and constraints drive the architecture; 2) Write measurable criteria: quality, p95, cost per success; 3) Ask data sensitivity, volume, and cost of a wrong answer early; 4) Interactive versus batch is a different product; 5) A missing latency budget makes a multi-call design illegal. The spoken close stays the same: I start from users, task, quality bar, p95, volume, cost, and data constraints, and I write measurable acceptance criteria before I name a model. Architecture is a consequence of those numbers, not the other way around.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

Write measurable criteria: quality, p95, cost per success.
Ask data sensitivity, volume, and cost of a wrong answer early.
Interactive versus batch is a different product.
A missing latency budget makes a multi-call design illegal.
Clarifying questions are scored in interviews.

questions.q: What questions do you ask before designing an AI feature?
questions.a: Users and task, input/output shape, quality bar and cost of errors, latency target, volume and peak, budget per request, data sensitivity and compliance, knowledge freshness, and whether a human can review. Then write measurable acceptance criteria.

questions.q: A PM says 'add an AI assistant to our app'. What do you do first?
questions.a: Do not choose tools. Clarify the user job, success metric, failure cost, latency and cost limits and data constraints, then define an eval set and thresholds. Only then compare prompting, RAG, agents or fine-tuning.

questions.q: A design uses a large model with five sequential calls for an autocomplete feature. What requirement was probably missed?
questions.a: The latency budget. Autocomplete needs well under a second, so five sequential large-model calls cannot fit. A p95 target would have forced a small model, one call, or caching.

questions.q: Why is cost of a wrong answer a first-class requirement?
questions.a: It decides whether you need citations, a human, or can ship a cheaper model. A wrong product name and a wrong dosage are not the same architecture.

questions.q: How do you turn 'be accurate' into an acceptance criterion?
questions.a: A labelled set of size n, a judge or human protocol, a threshold, and a date. Example: 90% on 200 cases, re-run on every release.

prompting-rag-agents-or-fine-tuning.explain:
## What it is

Four levers, ordered by cost and complexity. Pick the **cheapest that meets the acceptance criteria**. **Prompting** (instructions, examples, structured output) fixes behaviour, format, and tone. **RAG** adds knowledge the model lacks or that changes, with citations and easy updates. **Agents / tools** let the model choose actions when the path is not known in advance — more latency, cost, and failure modes. **Fine-tuning** changes behaviour, style, or distils a skill into a cheaper model; it does not reliably teach new facts.

Rule of thumb: missing knowledge → RAG; wrong behaviour or format → prompt, then fine-tune; unknown number of steps or side effects → agent. They combine: a small tuned model plus RAG plus one tool.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers probe the order you escalate. Fine-tuning to inject prices, or agents for a flowchart, are classic fails. On the job this ladder saves quarters.

## How it works + one small example

Example. 40-page policy that changes monthly, JSON out: prompt plus schema, RAG or long context, re-index on change. No tune, no agent. Example. Prices: a tool or retrieve-at-request-time, not a tune on last quarter. Example. Unknown lookups that depend on earlier results: a tool loop with step and cost limits.

## Failure modes

1. **Fine-tune for facts** that then go stale.

2. **Agents for a fixed pipeline.**

3. **RAG when the whole corpus fits** and never changes — maybe just context.

4. **Skipping the prompt** because tuning feels more serious.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I escalate prompt, RAG, tools or agents, then fine-tune, and I stop when the criteria are met. RAG is for knowledge; fine-tuning is for behaviour; agents are for unknown steps. I will not tune in last quarter's prices.

## A concrete walk-through

The team wants a multi-agent graph for FAQ. You run a prompted mid-size model plus retrieval on 200 cases: 88%. The gap is stale fees. You add a fee tool. 94%. You do not book GPUs.

## What I would measure

Features that skipped a cheaper lever; tunes whose failure was missing facts; agent loops that were later replaced by a flowchart.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for Four levers, ordered by cost and complexity. Pick the **cheapest that meets the  and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Escalate: prompt, RAG, tools/agents, fine-tune; 2) RAG is for knowledge; fine-tuning is for behaviour; 3) Agents only when steps cannot be fixed in advance; 4) They combine; they are not mutually exclusive; 5) Facts that change belong in retrieval or tools. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I escalate prompt, RAG, tools or agents, then fine-tune, and I stop when the criteria are met. RAG is for knowledge; fine-tuning is for behaviour; agents are for unknown steps. I will not tune in last quarter's prices.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.

RAG is for knowledge; fine-tuning is for behaviour.
Agents only when steps cannot be fixed in advance.
They combine; they are not mutually exclusive.
Facts that change belong in retrieval or tools.
Stop when acceptance criteria are met.

questions.q: When is RAG better than fine-tuning?
questions.a: When the need is knowledge that is private, large, or changing. RAG updates by editing the index, gives citations and access control, and avoids retraining. Fine-tuning suits behaviour, style, or distillation, not reliably adding facts.

questions.q: A bot must answer from a 40-page policy that changes monthly and always return JSON. Which levers?
questions.a: Prompting with a JSON schema for format and RAG (or long context) for the policy, re-indexed on change. No fine-tuning needed; maybe validation and retry. Agent loop unnecessary.

questions.q: Team fine-tuned a model on last quarter's pricing so it 'knows' prices. What breaks?
questions.a: Facts go stale and the model may still hallucinate prices; updating requires retraining. Prices should come from a tool or retrieval at request time.

questions.q: A task has an unknown number of lookups depending on earlier results. Which approach fits?
questions.a: A tool-using loop with step and cost limits. A single prompt cannot plan an unknown depth; a fully fixed graph may also fail if branches are data-dependent.

questions.q: When is fine-tuning the right next cost?
questions.a: When prompting cannot lock format or tone, you have labelled data and evals, volume justifies it, and facts still come from RAG or tools.

quality-latency-cost.explain:
## What it is

The central triangle: improving one usually spends another. **Quality** rises with bigger models, more context, retrieval, reranking, self-checks, and multiple samples. **Latency** rises with those too. **Cost** scales with tokens times volume (input and output priced separately), plus tools.

Typical moves: small model by default, escalate hard cases; **stream** to improve perceived latency; **cache**; trim context and cap output; parallelise independent calls (latency down, cost same). Identify the **binding constraint** (often p95 or a legal quality floor) and optimise the others around it. Averages hide the tail.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the language of every design review. Interviewers want the binding axis and three techniques that cut cost without a large quality loss. On the job, a 9 s p95 with a 1.2 s average is a product that feels broken.

## How it works + one small example

Worked (illustrative): large model costs 10× and takes 3×. If a small one handles 80% acceptably, blended cost is 0.8×1 + 0.2×10 = 2.8 versus 10, about 72% saved, hard 20% still get quality. Trace first: if decode dominates, cap output or stream; if retrieval dominates, shrink or cache; if TTFT dominates, cut prompt or cache the prefix.

## Failure modes

1. **Optimising average latency.**

2. **Quality with no cost or p95.**

3. **Parallelism** as a cost win — it is not.

4. **Streaming as a safety win** — it can leak before a check.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I name the binding constraint — usually p95 or a quality floor — then I use routing, caching, and context cuts around it. I measure cost per successful task and p95, not averages alone.

## A concrete walk-through

Tracing shows decode is 80% of a 5 s path. You cap output, stream, and route 70% to a small model. p95 falls under 4 s; the eval drops 1 point, still above the floor.

## What I would measure

p95 and p99 per route; cost per successful task; share routed to the small model; quality on the same eval after each change.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on The central triangle: improving one usually spends another. **Quality** rises wi, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Identify the binding constraint, then optimise the other two; 2) Routing and caching trade little quality for big cost wins; 3) Measure p95/p99 and cost per successful task; 4) Parallelism cuts latency, not cost; 5) Streaming helps perceived latency, not safety. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: I name the binding constraint — usually p95 or a quality floor — then I use routing, caching, and context cuts around it. I measure cost per successful task and p95, not averages alone.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.
keyPoints: Identify the binding constraint, then optimise the other two.
Routing and caching trade little quality for big cost wins.
Measure p95/p99 and cost per successful task.
Parallelism cuts latency, not cost.
Streaming helps perceived latency, not safety.
Trace before you guess which component dominates.

questions.q: Name three techniques that reduce cost without large quality loss.
questions.a: Route easy requests to a smaller model, cache repeated or prefix-stable work, trim context and cap output tokens. Prompt compression and batching offline work also help.

questions.q: Your assistant is accurate but p95 is 9 s and the target is 4 s. What options do you weigh?
questions.a: Stream for perceived latency, parallelise independent calls, shrink context, move easy cases to a faster model, cache. Trace which component dominates and re-eval quality after each change.

questions.q: A team reports 'average latency is 1.2 s, so we are fine' while users complain. What is wrong?
questions.a: Averages hide the tail. Slow requests (long contexts, retries, tool loops) dominate perception. Track p95/p99 per route and component.

questions.q: Why is blended routing often a ~70% cost win in the 80/20 case?
questions.a: Most traffic is easy. Paying 10× on 20% and 1× on 80% beats 10× on 100%. Illustrative: 2.8 versus 10 units. Measure on your mix.

questions.q: When must quality win the triangle?
questions.a: When the cost of a wrong answer is legal, medical, or financial. Then you spend latency and money, and you say so in the requirements.

## What it is

Start with the **simplest thing that could work**, measure it, and add complexity only where measurement shows a gap. A baseline might be one well-written prompt on a mid-size model, no retrieval, no agents, on a small golden set. Often it is close. Failure analysis tells you what to add: wrong facts → retrieval; wrong format → structured output; inconsistent behaviour → examples or a tune; multi-step → a fixed pipeline or a tool.

A **non-AI baseline** (rules, keyword search, template) is worth testing; sometimes it wins. Complex graphs have more failure modes and slower iteration. Every added component must prove quality gained versus latency and cost spent.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers want 'I would ship a baseline and an eval first'. On the job, this stops a quarter of platform work that does not move the number.

## How it works + one small example

Week 1: 150 labelled cases, one prompt, one model, a score. 78% versus 90% target. Failures are outdated facts — add retrieval, not agents. Re-run the same set. If you are at 89%, stop and ship. If format is the residue, add a schema, not a second agent.

## Failure modes

1. **Full architecture first**, no eval.

2. **Adding a reranker** because a talk mentioned it, with no ablation.

3. **Changing the eval** whenever the system looks bad.

4. **Ignoring the keyword-search baseline.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I ship a simple baseline and an eval set first, then I add the component the error analysis names. Each sophistication has to beat the baseline on quality per latency and cost. I will also try a non-LLM baseline.

## A concrete walk-through

You refuse the multi-agent design for a week. The baseline plus retrieval hits 91%. You ship it. The graph becomes a later experiment with an ablation plan.

## What I would measure

Ablations actually run; components with no quality delta still in prod; time from idea to a scored baseline.

questions.q: Why start with a baseline before a sophisticated architecture?
questions.a: It gives a measured reference so each added component must justify its latency, cost, and complexity, and error analysis shows what to add. It also ships value sooner.

questions.q: Baseline scores 78% on your eval set, target 90%. Failures are mostly outdated facts. Next step?
questions.a: Add retrieval or tool access to fresh sources, then re-run the same eval set. Do not add agents or fine-tuning; the error category is knowledge freshness.

questions.q: Why build an evaluation set before adding components to a baseline?
questions.a: So you can attribute quality changes to each component and stop when criteria are met. Without a fixed metric you cannot tell whether a reranker helped.

questions.q: A team added a graph and the score rose 2% while p95 doubled. What do you do?
questions.a: Ablate the new nodes. If the 2% is one component, keep that one. If none justify the latency, revert to the baseline plus that slice.

questions.q: When does a keyword-search baseline win?
questions.a: When queries are unique ids or exact titles and the LLM only wraps them. Ship search plus a template; do not pay for a 20-step agent.

**Latency, cost, privacy, and audit beat a fashionable diagram.** This item is the mindset: write the constraints on the board before the boxes. A graph of agents is not a design if it cannot meet 2 s p95, a $0.01 budget, a residency pin, or an audit of who approved a send. Components are how you meet constraints, not the starting vocabulary.

Fashionable means: multi-agent, 1M context, a new gateway, a fine-tune, a memory graph. Any of those can be right after the numbers exist. None of them are a first move.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you interrupt a whiteboard that started with 'we'll use framework X'. Interviewers reward the interruption.

## How it works + one small example

Order: constraints (p95, $, region, oversight) → levers (prompt/RAG/tools/tune) → components (which store, which model, which queue). ## Failure modes

1. **Diagram first, numbers later.**

2. **Copying last company's architecture.**

3. **Treating 1M context as free.**

4. **Privacy as an appendix.**

Constraints before components: I write p95, cost, privacy, and audit on the board first. A fashionable graph that misses those is not a design. Components are how I meet the numbers.

You write four numbers, then three boxes. The original twelve-box draft is in the appendix as 'rejected for p95 and residency'.

## What it is

**Ship retrieve-and-generate before agents or graphs.** This is the operational form of baseline-before-sophistication: the first production architecture is usually a prompt, a retriever, a validator, and a stream — not a planner. One sophistication means you add the *one* component the errors named (a reranker, a tool, a small tune), not a platform.

Agents and graphs are a later sophistication when the task is truly open-ended. Most internal copilots never need them.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is the sentence that keeps a v1 shippable. Interviewers use it to see if you can stop.

## How it works + one small example

v1: retrieve, generate, cite, validate JSON. v1.1: add a reranker if recall was the gap. v1.2: add a fee tool if facts were the gap. Do not add a supervisor agent in v1.1 'while we are in there'.

## Failure modes

1. **Platform in v1.**

2. **Two sophistications at once**, so you cannot attribute.

3. **Calling a graph the baseline** because the tutorial started there.

I ship retrieve-and-generate first, then I add one sophistication the errors named. Agents and graphs wait until the task is actually open-ended. Two changes at once are not an experiment.

## A concrete walk-through

v1 ships in two weeks: RAG plus schema. The graph stays on a branch until a labelled set of multi-step cases exists and fails the pipeline.

I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) v1 is retrieve-and-generate, not a graph; 2) Add one component per iteration; 3) Agents wait for truly open-ended tasks; 4) Two changes at once cannot be attributed; 5) A tutorial graph is not a baseline. The spoken close stays the same: I ship retrieve-and-generate first, then I add one sophistication the errors named. Agents and graphs wait until the task is actually open-ended. Two changes at once are not an experiment.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

questions.a: Retrieve, generate, cite, validate. Not a multi-agent graph.

questions.q: Why only one sophistication at a time?
questions.a: So you can attribute the quality and latency change. Two at once is a guess.

questions.a: When error analysis shows an unknown number of tool steps that a fixed pipeline cannot express, and the eval still misses that slice.

questions.a: Ignore it for v1. Tutorials optimise for showing the framework, not for your p95.

questions.a: Eval score versus target, residual error categories, and a written 'we will not add X until Y'.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: 30-minute design** is a spoken agenda: **requirements, options, pick, trade-offs, eval, and what you would cut**. You spend the first minutes on requirements (this module), you list two or three options on the ladder, you pick one against the numbers, you name what you spent on the triangle, you describe the eval set, and you say what you drop if the deadline moves a week left.

That agenda is the product of M9.1. If you start drawing a gateway in minute two, you failed the agenda even if the gateway is good.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how staff interviews are scored. The agenda is the skill. On the job it is the same six headings in a design doc.

## How it works + one small example

Minute 0–8: questions and numbers. 8–14: options (prompt+RAG vs agent vs tune). 14–20: pick and diagram the minimum. 20–25: trade-offs and failure modes. 25–28: eval and rollout. 28–30: cut list. Practise with a timer.

## Failure modes

1. **Drawing first.**

2. **No cut list.**

3. **No eval.**

4. **One option** so there is no pick.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

In a 30-minute design I do requirements, options, pick, trade-offs, eval, and what I would cut. I spend the first minutes on numbers, and I will not start with a fashionable diagram.

where-knowledge-should-come-from.explain:
## What it is

Decide, per fact type, whether knowledge lives in the **model**, the **prompt**, **RAG**, **memory**, or a **tool / database**. Model knowledge is parametric, stale, and uncited. Prompt knowledge is small and always-on (the style guide, the output schema). RAG is large, changing, or private text you can cite and ACL. Memory is user- or session-specific state. Tools and DBs are live, authoritative values (order status, price, inventory).

The decision is a table, not a vibe. Current order status is a tool. The refund policy is RAG (or a snapshot). Tone is a prompt or a tune. The user's preferred language is memory. 'What is a vector database' can stay in the model.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers ask 'where does knowledge live' and expect this table. On the job, putting live prices in a tune or a 40-page policy in every prompt is how systems rot.

## How it works + one small example

For each field: freshness SLA, size, ACL, need to cite, write rate. Example: order status — seconds-fresh, tiny, per-user, must be exact → `get_order`. Policy — weekly, 40 pages, company-wide, must cite → index. Brand voice — yearly, small → prompt or tune.

## Failure modes

1. **One store for everything.**

2. **Fine-tune for the CMS.**

3. **Memory as a junk drawer** of facts that should be retrieved.

4. **Model knowledge for regulated claims.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I place knowledge on purpose: model for stable generalities, prompt for small standing rules, RAG for large or changing documents, memory for per-user state, and tools for live authoritative values. I will not tune in this week's prices.

## A concrete walk-through

You draw four buckets on the board and place ten facts. Prices move to a tool; the policy to RAG; tone to the prompt. The tune proposal dies.

## What I would measure

Facts with a written home; incidents of stale parametric answers; prompt tokens spent on documents that should have been retrieved.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on Decide, per fact type, whether knowledge lives in the **model**, the **prompt**, is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Choose model, prompt, RAG, memory, or tool per fact type; 2) Live authoritative values belong in tools or DBs; 3) Changing or private documents belong in RAG; 4) Small standing rules belong in the prompt; 5) Memory is per-user state, not a second CMS. The spoken close stays the same: I place knowledge on purpose: model for stable generalities, prompt for small standing rules, RAG for large or changing documents, memory for per-user state, and tools for live authoritative values. I will not tune in this week's prices.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

## What it is

Design the pipeline as **ingestion → retrieval → reranking → context assembly → generation** (then validation). Ingestion: parse, chunk, ACL, embed, store provenance. Retrieval: hybrid search under a permission filter. Rerank: a cross-encoder or a small model on the shortlist. Assembly: budgets, wrapping data as data, citations ids. Generation: the model. Each stage has an owner, an SLA, and a way to fail closed. Skipping a stage is a decision (no rerank if n is tiny), not an accident.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

## How it works + one small example

## Failure modes

2. **Retrieve without ACL.**

## What it is

**Vector, keyword, and graph** (and others) catch different queries. Dense vectors miss exact ids (`E4021`) and rare tokens. Keyword (BM25) misses paraphrase. Graph helps when the question is about relationships ('who owns the service that depends on X'). Combine when the eval says so, usually via **hybrid retrieve + fusion** (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) then a rerank.

Do not combine because a slide had three logos. Each extra index has an ingest and an ACL story.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Misses cluster on SKUs and error codes. You add BM25, fuse with RRF, and the slice recovers 12 points. You do not add a graph.

freshness-access-control-provenance.explain:
## What it is

Three production properties of knowledge: **freshness** (how stale is allowed, who updates), **access control** (retrieval is a security boundary), and **provenance** (what span, which version). They belong in the architecture, not in a later 'ops' slide. Freshness is an SLA: policy weekly, orders seconds, web crawl daily. Access control is the mandatory filter. Provenance is ids and hashes in the prompt and the trace.

If any of the three is missing, you cannot safely scale the corpus.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the enterprise bar for RAG. Interviewers will ask all three in one breath.

## How it works + one small example

Write SLAs next to each corpus. Policy: snapshot id in the card, rebuild on merge, TTL on chunks. Orders: no index, live tool. Access: session tenant on every query. Provenance: citation required to emit a policy claim.

## Failure modes

1. **Crawl with no freshness SLA.**

2. **ACL as a helper.**

3. **Answers with no source.**

4. **A snapshot dated in the UI, a different one in the index.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Freshness, access control, and provenance are architecture. I give each corpus an SLA, I filter before retrieve, and I keep ids and versions on every chunk and citation.

## A concrete walk-through

You add a `freshness.md` table and a CI test that HR retrieve uses the reviewed snapshot id. A stale-policy incident becomes a missed rebuild, not a mystery.

## What I would measure

Corpora with an SLA; ACL tests; citation rate; snapshot-id mismatches.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on Three production properties of knowledge: **freshness** (how stale is allowed, w, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Every corpus has a freshness SLA and an owner; 2) Access control is a retrieve-time boundary; 3) Provenance is id, version, hash, span; 4) Live data should not go stale in an index; 5) The UI snapshot date must match the index. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: Freshness, access control, and provenance are architecture. I give each corpus an SLA, I filter before retrieve, and I keep ids and versions on every chunk and citation.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.
keyPoints: Every corpus has a freshness SLA and an owner.
Access control is a retrieve-time boundary.
Provenance is id, version, hash, span.
Live data should not go stale in an index.
The UI snapshot date must match the index.
You cannot scale a corpus that lacks these three.

questions.a: At retrieve time, in the query, with the principal from the session — before ANN or via filtered search. Not in the prompt.

questions.a: Name an owner and an SLA per corpus: policy weekly with a snapshot id, orders live via a tool, crawl daily. Write it in the design.

questions.q: A support copilot quotes an outdated refund policy after an update. Most direct fix?
questions.a: Rebuild or invalidate that snapshot, bust caches, and show the snapshot date. Do not prompt the model to 'be current'.

questions.q: Why is provenance part of this trio, not only UX?
questions.a: You cannot takedown, erase, or defend a claim without it.

questions.a: The assembler injects the snapshot id from the same config the index uses. A test compares them.

## What it is

Always-present: role, output shape, current goal, the tool list for this task, a tiny policy summary. Retrieved: large or situational documents, old threads, code files. The class is a property of the content: how often needed, how large, how costly a miss. Small and almost always needed stays resident. Large or rare is retrieved. If a miss is catastrophic, keep a short always-present version and retrieve the rest.

You cut the always-on policy from 4k to 400 tokens, retrieve the rest, and p95 drops 800 ms with no eval loss on the clause set.

questions.a: A short always-present summary plus retrieval of the relevant clauses, or a cached snapshot if eval shows the full 4k is worth the TTFT. Measure; do not default to stuffing.

questions.a: Role, safety, output shape, current goal, this-task tools, and a tiny standing summary. Not the whole corpus.

## What it is

**Who updates the corpus and how stale is allowed** is a written SLA, not a hope. Each corpus: owner, update trigger (merge, cron, event), maximum age, and what users see when it is stale (banner, refuse, degrade). Policy might be 'within 4 hours of merge'. Prices are 'not in the corpus'. Web crawl is '24 h, banner if older'.

Without an SLA, 'we have RAG' means 'we have a pile of unknown vintage'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the ops contract that makes RAG believable. Interviewers ask who pages when the policy is old.

## How it works + one small example

Table in the repo. Alerts when `now - snapshot.time > SLA`. The UI shows the snapshot time on policy answers. A missed rebuild is a page, not a user tweet.

## Failure modes

1. **No owner.**

2. **No banner** when stale.

3. **Mixing SLAs** in one index so you cannot expire one corpus.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every corpus has a freshness SLA: an owner, a trigger, a maximum age, and a user-visible stale behaviour. I page on a missed rebuild. 'We have RAG' is not a freshness story.

## A concrete walk-through

You add `snapshot_age_seconds` to the dashboard and a page at 4 h. The first page finds a broken webhook. That is the SLA working.

## What I would measure

SLA breaches; time-to-rebuild; UI answers missing a snapshot time.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for **Who updates the corpus and how stale is allowed** is a written SLA, not a hope and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Owner, trigger, max age, stale behaviour — per corpus; 2) Show snapshot time on policy answers; 3) Page when age exceeds the SLA; 4) Do not mix unlike SLAs in one indistinguishable pile; 5) Prices usually have no corpus SLA because they are live. The sentence I can say under pressure is: Every corpus has a freshness SLA: an owner, a trigger, a maximum age, and a user-visible stale behaviour. I page on a missed rebuild. 'We have RAG' is not a freshness story.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.
## A note on residual risk

I treat leftover risk on **who updates the corpus and how stale is allowed** is a written sla, not a hope as something I can name, not as a vibe. If a control is probabilistic I say the residual attack or error rate. If a number is missing I write the smallest measurement that would change my mind. I would rather ship a smaller surface with a written residual than a larger one I cannot explain. The owner of that residual is a person, and the review date is on a calendar.

questions.a: Owner, update trigger, maximum age, and what the user sees when stale.

questions.q: How do users know a policy answer might be stale?
questions.a: A snapshot timestamp and a banner or refuse when the SLA is breached. Do not hide it.

access-control-as-architecture.explain:
## What it is

**Retrieval is a security boundary, not a helper.** This is the system-design restatement of Level 8's ACL rule. The retrieve box on the diagram has a lock. The query builder cannot be called without a principal. Caches inherit the key. Design reviews treat a missing lock like a missing auth on an HTTP route.

If someone says 'the model will not quote other tenants', the architecture is already wrong.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is the sentence that keeps RAG out of a security incident. Interviewers listen for 'boundary', not 'we filter sometimes'.

## How it works + one small example

## What it is

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

## How it works + one small example

## Failure modes

1. **RAG for everything.**

2. **No 'why not the others'.**

3. **Forgetting ACL when you say index.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I answer where knowledge lives with a table: prompt, index, database, or fine-tune, and why not the others. Freshness, ACL, and citations follow the home I chose. 'We will use RAG' is not an answer.

## A concrete walk-through

You write a 3×4 table in one minute and sit back. That is the item.

## What I would measure

Practice answers that include 'why not'; designs whose facts have a home.

## What it is

A **model gateway** is the internal service between your apps and one or more LLM providers. Apps call a provider-neutral API; the gateway owns the rest: unified schema, **routing** and fallbacks, **auth and keys** (apps never hold provider keys), **rate limits and quotas** per team or feature, **observability** (latency, tokens, cost, model version, trace ids), **policy** (redaction, allow-listed models, region pin), **caching**, retries, timeouts, and request shaping.

Without it every service reimplements retries and keys, costs are invisible, and a deprecation is a many-team fire drill. With it, swapping a model is a config change.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the first box in a production design. Interviewers ask why not call the vendor from each service. On the job it is how you survive a model retirement.

## How it works + one small example

## Failure modes

1. **Keys in each microservice.**

2. **No usage attribution** so one batch job surprises finance.

3. **A 'gateway' that is only a reverse proxy** with no policy or quotas.

4. **Every team on the latest alias** with no pin.

The gateway is the abstraction between apps and providers: keys, routing, limits, retries, policy, and usage. Apps call a stable internal API; swapping a model is a config change. I hide keys and I pin snapshots.

You move three services behind the gateway, delete two leaked keys, and survive a vendor deprecation with a config PR and a re-eval.

questions.a: One place to change the model map. Apps keep calling the same internal route. You re-eval, then flip config.

questions.a: To prevent leakage, to rotate in one place, and to enforce policy before the vendor sees the call.

## What it is

**Route** requests by **task type, capability, latency, context length, cost, modality, or risk** — not by whichever model the author liked. Classification and easy FAQ go cheap and fast. Long-context summarisation needs a large window. High-stakes legal advice needs a strong model, a grounded path, and a fallback that is **safe** (human or refuse), not merely cheaper.

Routing signals are features of the request: length, language, tool need, data class, user tier. They are not a second model guessing for fun unless you measured that guess.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you spend the triangle on purpose. Interviewers distinguish routing signals from cascade signals.

## How it works + one small example

Table: `support.faq` → small, cached; `support.refund` → mid + tools + approval; `legal.draft` → large + RAG + no cheap fallback; `image.alt` → vision model. Risk is a first-class column: if risk is high, do not fail over to a toy model that will cheerfully hallucinate.

## Failure modes

1. **One model for all routes.**

2. **Cheapest fallback on a high-risk route.**

3. **Routing on user id** as a proxy for difficulty.

4. **A router model** that costs more than it saves.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I route on task, cost, and risk. Easy work goes to small and fast models; high-risk work goes to a grounded strong path and a safe fallback — not a cheaper hallucination. Routing is a table, not a favourite model.

## A concrete walk-through

You publish the route table. Legal loses its cheap fallback. FAQ gets a small model. The bill drops and the scary route gets safer.

## What I would measure

Share of traffic per route; high-risk fallbacks that were cheap models; router overhead.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on **Route** requests by **task type, capability, latency, context length, cost, mo is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Route on task, capability, latency, window, cost, modality, risk; 2) High-risk routes do not fail over to a toy model; 3) Routing signals come from the request, not from taste; 4) A router must save more than it costs; 5) Write the table; do not keep it in someone's head. The spoken close stays the same: I route on task, cost, and risk. Easy work goes to small and fast models; high-risk work goes to a grounded strong path and a safe fallback — not a cheaper hallucination. Routing is a table, not a favourite model.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

High-risk routes do not fail over to a toy model.
Routing signals come from the request, not from taste.
A router must save more than it costs.
Write the table; do not keep it in someone's head.
Data class is a routing signal (residency, ZDR).

questions.a: It constrains both the primary model and the fallback. High risk narrows the set to grounded, logged, possibly human-reviewed paths.

## What it is

A **cascade** tries a **cheaper or faster model first** and escalates to a stronger one when the easy path is not good enough. The escalate signal can be the small model's self-reported confidence (weak), a validator (schema, grounding, classifier), or a cheap second pass. Cascades win when **most requests are easy**.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Escalate rate is 18% on FAQ and the blended cost is a third of always-large. You keep it. On legal it is 70%; you remove the cascade.

a-cascade-that-fails-open-to-a-safe-defa.explain:
## What it is

**Cheap model first; escalate; never silently drop the schema.** This is the slogan form of a safe cascade. Fail-open here means fail toward a **safe** next action — a stronger model, a template, a human, a clear error — not toward an untyped string because parsing failed.

'Open' is easy to misread as 'let it through'. In this item it means the cascade does not dead-end in a corrupt payload. The default is safe and typed.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers listen for 'never drop the schema'. On the job this is the bug where a mobile client crashes on a missing field during a cascade.

## How it works + one small example

If small model JSON fails: escalate. If large also fails: return a versioned error object the client understands, or a templated safe reply. Never `{}` or a prose apology where a machine expected fields.

## Failure modes

1. **Coercing invalid JSON.**

2. **Prose where a schema was promised.**

3. **Calling fail-open 'return the raw text'.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A safe cascade is cheap first, escalate on a check, and never silently drop the schema. The default is a typed error, a stronger model, or a template — not an untyped apology.

## A concrete walk-through

You add a contract test on both hops. A chaos day that breaks the small model still returns valid JSON or a 422 the client handles.

## What I would measure

Schema-violating responses; cascade hops without a contract test.

I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What it is

**The gateway is where keys and budgets live, not in each service.** This item is the short form of centralising auth. Keys: one vault, short-lived if the vendor allows, never in app env files. ## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is the sentence security and finance both want. Interviewers use it to see if you have operated a gateway.

Vault → gateway at boot or via sidecar. Quota config as code. Interactive routes reserved capacity. Batch borrows leftovers. A 429 from the vendor is mapped to your quota language so apps do not retry on their own.

2. **One budget for batch and chat.**

You pull keys from six repos into the vault and add two quotas. The nightly embed job no longer pages the chat SLO.

## What it is

**Streaming** sends tokens as they are produced so **time-to-first-token** becomes the perceived wait. Total generation time may stay the same; users forgive a long answer if it starts quickly. ## What it is

If two pieces of work do not depend on each other, run them concurrently so latency is the **max, not the sum**. Common: several retrievals, independent tool calls, guardrails alongside generation (cancel if the guard trips), embed-while-load, section generation for a report. Illustrative: three 400 ms lookups go from 1.2 s to ~400 ms.

Parallelism **does not cut cost** and can raise it (speculative work you throw away). Watch rate limits and partial failure: timeouts, proceed with what returned, or fail if a required source missed.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is free latency if you were sequential by habit. Interviewers will give you three lookups.

## How it works + one small example

2. **Unbounded fan-out** into 429s.

3. **Calling parallelism a cost win.**

## What it is

**Prompt and context reduction**, **batching**, and **inference-service** tricks (quantisation, speculative decoding, prefix cache) cut both TTFT and cost. Reduction: drop unused tools, summarise history, retrieve less, cap output. Batching: offline jobs and some embeddings share a batch; interactive chat usually cannot wait for a batch. Service tricks are what you ask a platform team for after you have cut the prompt.

Do reduction first. It is under your control and it helps every model.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

prefill-vs-decode-costs.explain:
## What it is

**Long prompts hurt TTFT; long outputs hurt tokens and time.** Prefill (reading the prompt) is compute-heavy and grows with input length; it dominates TTFT. Decode is stepwise and grows with output length; it dominates total time and often the bill (output tokens are priced higher on many APIs). The optimisation is different: cut or cache input versus cap or steer output.

A 20k-token RAG dump with a 20-token answer is a prefill problem. A 800-token prompt with a 2k-token essay is a decode problem. Do not apply the same fix to both.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the mental model behind every latency and cost ticket. Interviewers will give you one of each.

## How it works + one small example

Read the trace: if TTFT is huge and complete is only a bit larger, prefill. If TTFT is fine and the stream crawls, decode. Fixes: prefix cache and retrieve-less versus `max_tokens`, tighter instructions, and a smaller model on decode-heavy routes.

## Failure modes

1. **One 'make it faster' ticket** with no split.

2. **Caching output** when the problem was prefill.

3. **Raising max_tokens** 'to be safe' on a decode-heavy route.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Long prompts hurt TTFT (prefill); long outputs hurt time and money (decode). I read the trace, I apply the matching fix, and I do not raise max_tokens to be safe on a decode-heavy route.

## A concrete walk-through

Two tickets, two fixes: you cache a 8k prefix; you drop max_tokens from 4k to 512 on FAQ. Both p95s move for different reasons.

## What I would measure

TTFT versus input length; complete time versus output tokens; max_tokens by route.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on **Long prompts hurt TTFT; long outputs hurt tokens and time.** Prefill (reading  is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Prefill scales with input and drives TTFT; 2) Decode scales with output and drives total time and often cost; 3) Different fixes: cache/cut input vs cap output; 4) Read the trace before you pick a fix; 5) Output tokens are often priced higher. ## What it is

Caching spends **freshness** to buy **latency and cost**. That trade is explicit: a 10-minute FAQ cache is usually fine; a 10-minute price cache is not; a 10-minute policy cache after a legal change is a bug. Draw the curve: hit rate versus staleness versus dollars. Pick a point per route.

When freshness is the binding constraint, you cache prefixes and retrieval of unchanged docs, not answers. When cost is binding and content is stable, you cache answers aggressively.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the triangle applied to caches. Interviewers want a per-route answer, not 'cache everything 24h'.

## How it works + one small example

FAQ: answer cache 1–6 h plus prefix cache. Prices: no answer cache; maybe a 30 s retrieval cache on the catalog if the system of record agrees. Policy: answer cache with instant bust on publish. Measure freshness incidents separately from hit rate.

## Failure modes

1. **One TTL for the product.**

2. **Celebrating hit rate** during a stale-policy incident.

3. **Answer-caching live data.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Caching trades freshness for latency and cost. I pick the point per route: aggressive on stable FAQ, instant-bust on policy, none on live prices. Hit rate is not success if the answer is stale.

## A concrete walk-through

You split TTLs: FAQ 3 h, policy event-bust, prices off. Finance still sees a prefix-cache saving. Legal stops paging you.

## What I would measure

Stale-hit rate; TTL by route; prefix-cache savings on no-answer-cache routes.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for Caching spends **freshness** to buy **latency and cost**. That trade is explicit and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) The trade is freshness versus latency and cost; 2) Pick a point per route, not one TTL; 3) Live values: do not cache answers; 4) Policy: cache with instant bust; 5) Hit rate during a stale incident is a vanity metric. The sentence I can say under pressure is: Caching trades freshness for latency and cost. I pick the point per route: aggressive on stable FAQ, instant-bust on policy, none on live prices. Hit rate is not success if the answer is stale.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.

measuring-the-hit-rate.explain:
## What it is

**Measure actual hit rate and savings**, do not assume. Hit rate is hits/(hits+misses) **per cache and per route**, plus **dollars and milliseconds saved**, plus **error rate on hits**. A 70% hit rate that saves 2% of cost is not the same as a 30% hit rate that saves 40% because it hits the expensive prefix.

Also measure **false hits** (semantic wrong, stale, leaked). A cache you do not measure will be turned off in a panic after one incident, or left on forever after it dies.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the anti-handwave item. Interviewers ask how you know caching helped.

## How it works + one small example

Dashboard: hit rate, p95 with and without (shadow or holdout), $ saved, stale-hit, leak canaries. A weekly read. If prefix cache reports hits but the bill did not move, you are caching the wrong bytes.

## Failure modes

1. **One global hit rate.**

2. **No $ column.**

3. **No holdout**, so you cannot prove causality.

4. **Ignoring false hits.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I measure hit rate, dollars and milliseconds saved, and error on hits — per cache and route. I do not assume caching helped, and I will not celebrate a hit rate that did not move the bill.

## A concrete walk-through

You add $ saved next to hit rate. The semantic cache is 55% hits and $12/day. The prefix cache is 40% hits and $400/day. You fund prefix stability, not a lower semantic threshold.

## What I would measure

Dashboards with $ and false-hit; holdouts run; caches without a route tag.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on **Measure actual hit rate and savings**, do not assume. Hit rate is hits/(hits+m, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Hit rate per cache and per route; 2) Report $ and ms saved, not only percent; 3) Track false hits: stale, wrong, leaked; 4) A holdout proves causality; 5) Global averages hide a dead cache. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: I measure hit rate, dollars and milliseconds saved, and error on hits — per cache and route. I do not assume caching helped, and I will not celebrate a hit rate that did not move the bill.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.

questions.a: One route can dominate or a cheap cache can look healthy while the expensive prefix never hits.

questions.a: Hit rate, $ or ms saved, and error/stale/leak rate on hits.

questions.a: A cache return that is stale, for the wrong tenant, or semantically wrong. Count it against the cache, not as a win.

semantic-cache-invalidation.explain:
## What it is

**A new policy doc must bust similar questions, not just exact matches.** Semantic invalidation is the hard part: entries are keyed by embeddings, not by `doc_id`. Strategies: store the cited doc ids on each entry and drop intersections; flush the whole route; reduce TTL on policy routes; re-embed a tombstone query set and drop neighbours.

If you cannot do this, do not semantic-cache policy answers. Exact-plus-prefix is enough.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the item that separates a demo cache from a legal-safe one. Interviewers will mention a policy update.

## How it works + one small example

On publish of `doc_id=P`, delete cache rows where `cited_ids contains P` or `route=policy`. If you did not store cited ids, you cannot do the first — so store them. Test: publish a canary sentence, ask a paraphrase, assert miss then a new hit with the new sentence.

## Failure modes

1. **No cited_ids on the entry.**

2. **Exact-key delete only.**

3. **Semantic-caching policy** without a bust path.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A new policy doc must bust similar questions, not just exact matches. I store cited doc ids on semantic entries, I drop intersections on publish, and if I cannot, I do not semantic-cache that route.

## A concrete walk-through

You add `cited_ids` and a publish hook. The paraphrase test goes green. Policy stays on semantic cache with a bust you can explain.

## What I would measure

Time-to-bust on paraphrase; entries missing cited_ids; policy routes without a hook.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for **A new policy doc must bust similar questions, not just exact matches.** Semant and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Exact delete does not bust paraphrases; 2) Store cited doc ids on each semantic entry; 3) Publish hooks drop intersections or flush the route; 4) If you cannot bust, do not semantic-cache policy; 5) Test with a paraphrase after publish. The sentence I can say under pressure is: A new policy doc must bust similar questions, not just exact matches. I store cited doc ids on semantic entries, I drop intersections on publish, and if I cannot, I do not semantic-cache that route.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.

questions.a: Only as a backstop. Legal changes should not wait five minutes.

what-you-must-never-cache.explain:
## What it is

**Personalized or secret answers in a shared key** — that is the never. Also never: credentials, raw PII you would not log, someone else's tenant data, one-time links, and high-risk advice that must be re-grounded every time. The never is about the **combination** of data class and key scope. A personal answer in a **user-scoped** cache with a short TTL can be fine. The same answer under `hash(question)` is an incident.

Write the nevers in the gateway. Make them tests.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the interview line they want in one breath. On the job it is the code comment that stops a helpful engineer.

## How it works + one small example

Denylist: routes tagged `personalized` or `secret` cannot use semantic or global exact cache. CI greps for cache middleware on those routes. A canary user asks 'what is my balance' after another user did; expect miss.

## Failure modes

1. **'It is only FAQ'** that sometimes includes an account number.

2. **User-scoped intended**, global implemented.

3. **Caching 2FA codes** because they look like short answers.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I never cache personalised or secret answers on a shared key. User-scoped short TTL can be OK; `hash(question)` is not. The never is a tested denylist, not a comment.

## A concrete walk-through

You tag `/me/*` as personalised. A PR that adds semantic cache there fails CI. That is the never as code.

## What I would measure

Personal routes with a shared cache; canary leaks; 2FA-like strings in cache dumps.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on **Personalized or secret answers in a shared key** — that is the never. Also nev is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Never: personal or secret answers on a shared key; 2) Also never: creds, one-time links, other tenants; 3) User-scoped cache is a different design; 4) The combination of data class and key scope is the bug; 5) Denylist routes in the gateway with tests. The spoken close stays the same: I never cache personalised or secret answers on a shared key. User-scoped short TTL can be OK; `hash(question)` is not. The never is a tested denylist, not a comment.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

Also never: creds, one-time links, other tenants.
User-scoped cache is a different design.
The combination of data class and key scope is the bug.
Denylist routes in the gateway with tests.
FAQ that sometimes includes an account number is not FAQ.

questions.a: Personalised or secret answers under a shared key — plus credentials, one-time tokens, and other tenants' data.

questions.a: When the key includes the user, the TTL is short, and the store is isolated. Not on a global semantic cache.

questions.a: They are secrets and time-bound. A cache turns them into a theft and a UX bug.

designing-for-every-failure.explain:
## What it is

Design for **model failures, provider outages, tool failures, rate limits, malformed outputs, and retrieval misses** — not only the happy path. Each has a behaviour: retry with jitter, fall back, degrade, refuse, or queue. 'The model will behave' is not a design. A missing retrieval should not become a confident essay; a 429 should not become a 30-second client retry storm; a tool timeout should not leave a half-applied write.

Write the matrix: failure × response. That matrix is the reliability spec.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the difference between a demo and a service. Interviewers will kill a dependency and watch what you do.

## How it works + one small example

Matrix rows: provider 5xx, provider 429, timeout, invalid JSON, retrieve empty, tool 5xx, guard timeout. Columns: retry?, fallback?, user message, page?. Example: retrieve empty → 'I could not find a source' plus search links, not a guessed policy.

## Failure modes

1. **Happy path only.**

2. **Retry everything 12 times.**

3. **Guessing when retrieval is empty.**

4. **No page** on a silent degrade that lasts an hour.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I design for model, provider, tool, rate-limit, schema, and retrieval failures with an explicit matrix. Empty retrieval does not become a confident essay, and a 429 does not become a retry storm.

## A concrete walk-through

You add the matrix to the design doc. Chaos day hits retrieve-empty and 429. The bot says it cannot find a source; chat does not melt. Two matrix cells were empty — those are the tickets.

## What I would measure

Matrix cells with no owner; retrieve-empty that still produced a policy claim; unbounded retries in code.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on Design for **model failures, provider outages, tool failures, rate limits, malfo is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Write a failure × response matrix; 2) Cover model, provider, tools, 429s, schema, retrieval; 3) Empty retrieve must not hallucinate a policy; 4) Retries are bounded and deadline-aware; 5) Some failures page; some degrade quietly. The spoken close stays the same: I design for model, provider, tool, rate-limit, schema, and retrieval failures with an explicit matrix. Empty retrieval does not become a confident essay, and a 429 does not become a retry storm.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

questions.a: Refuse or degrade to search/human — do not let the model invent the policy. Log the miss.

questions.a: Bounded retries with jitter, sharing the remaining deadline, then a per-route fallback. Not an unbounded client loop.

questions.a: Page when interactive SLOs or high-risk routes fail. Quietly degrade a non-critical rewrite feature to passthrough.

LLMs make some retries expensive and some writes non-idempotent (a second refund). The kit is the same; the settings are not nginx defaults.

2. **Retrying a non-idempotent refund.**

I put timeouts, bounded jittered retries, circuit breakers, queues, and rate limits on every LLM and tool hop, and I do not retry a non-idempotent write. Defaults from a web client are wrong here.

## A concrete walk-through

You add deadlines and a breaker. The next vendor blip becomes a 10-second degrade, not a thread-pool death.

questions.a: So you do not start a 2 s call when 100 ms remains on the user SLO. Fail instead.

questions.q: When must you not retry?
questions.a: Non-idempotent writes (refund, send) without a key, and when the breaker is open.

questions.a: Fast failure and room to degrade instead of stacking threads and cost on a dead vendor.

guardrails-at-system-boundaries.explain:
## What it is

Place **guardrails at system boundaries**, not only inside the model: input to the app, retrieve, model I/O, **action** (the important one), and renderer. Enforcement of 'human approval before refund' lives in the executor, not in a sentence. Schema checks live on the way out of the model. ACL lives on retrieve. XSS controls live on the renderer.

A boundary guard is deterministic when it can be. The model is allowed to help with classification; it is not allowed to be the only lock on money.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This restates Level 8 in system-design language. Interviewers ask where the refund rule lives.

## How it works + one small example

Diagram locks on five lines. Tests call the executor with a hostile model output and expect deny. Prompt text may mention the rule; the test does not read the prompt.

## Failure modes

1. **Refund limit in the prompt only.**

2. **Guards only at the chat box.**

3. **Renderer with no lock** because 'it is just markdown'.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Guardrails sit on boundaries: input, retrieve, model I/O, action, renderer. The refund rule lives in the executor. I test with a hostile model output and I expect deny.

## A concrete walk-through

You move the refund limit into the executor and add a hostile-output test. The prompt sentence stays as a hint.

## What I would measure

human-approval-for-high-risk-actions.explain:
## What it is

**Human approval for high-risk or irreversible actions** is a reliability and a safety control: it is how you fail closed when the model is down, unsure, or dangerous. The pending-action design from Level 8 belongs in the system diagram here. High-risk is a labelled set: send, pay, delete, deploy, legal send-outs.

Reliability angle: if the model is degraded, those actions stay behind the same gate; they do not flip to auto because the validator timed out.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

System-design interviews must not 'forget' the human when they talk SLOs. On the job, fail-open on approval is an outage-shaped incident.

## How it works + one small example

Risk label on the route. Executor requires `approval_id`. Guard timeout → no action. Degraded mode cannot skip the gate. SLOs for approval wait are separate from generation SLOs.

## Failure modes

1. **Auto-approve when the judge is down.**

2. **No pending object.**

3. **Mixing approval wait into the generation p95** and then removing approval to 'hit the SLO'.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

High-risk actions stay behind a human gate even when the model or a judge is down. I do not fail open to auto-send to save an SLO, and I measure approval wait separately from generation p95.

## A concrete walk-through

A judge outage used to auto-send. You flip it to fail closed. Refund p95 looks worse; incidents look better. You split the SLOs.

## What I would measure

High-risk actions without approval_id; fail-open events; generation SLO that still includes human wait.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on **Human approval for high risk or irreversible actions** is a reliability and a , I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) High-risk set is labelled and gated; 2) Guard or model down → no auto-action; 3) Approval wait has its own SLO; 4) Do not drop the gate to hit generation p95; 5) Pending objects, not chat vapour. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: High-risk actions stay behind a human gate even when the model or a judge is down. I do not fail open to auto-send to save an SLO, and I measure approval wait separately from generation p95.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.
keyPoints: High-risk set is labelled and gated.
Guard or model down → no auto-action.
Approval wait has its own SLO.
Do not drop the gate to hit generation p95.
Pending objects, not chat vapour.
Reliability and safety share this control.

questions.a: Fail closed: no refund, retry or human. Do not auto-send to save latency.

questions.q: Why separate approval-wait SLO from generation p95?
questions.a: So you do not delete the gate to make a latency dashboard green. Humans take seconds to minutes.

questions.a: The same gate is the fail-closed path when models or judges are sick.
