questions.a: No. Degraded mode may disable generation; it may not enable writes.

questions.q: Where is the gate on the system diagram?
questions.a: On the arrow from executor to the side-effecting system, labelled 'approval_id required'.

service-level-expectations.explain:
## What it is

Define **SLOs for availability, latency, and quality** — not only uptime. An LLM feature can be 100% up and 40% wrong. Quality SLOs use an online sample, a judge calibrated to humans, or a golden-set replay. Latency SLOs use p95 per route. Availability is 'usefully serving the intended path', not 'the process is up'.

Page on what users feel: error rate, p95, and a quality burn. Do not page on 'the vibe dropped' and do not skip quality because it is hard.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you operate the system after the design interview. Interviewers ask what you page on.

## How it works + one small example

Examples: availability 99.5% useful responses; p95 3 s on FAQ; citation-valid ≥ 90% on a 5% sample. Error budget: you can ship risky changes until quality or p95 burns the budget. A 100% uptime week with a citation crash is a failed week.

## Failure modes

1. **Uptime-only SLO.**

2. **Quality with no sample.**

3. **Paging on GPU utilisation.**

4. **One SLO for all routes.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I set SLOs on availability, p95, and quality, and I page on error rate and p95 — not on vibe or GPU utilisation. 100% uptime with wrong answers is a miss.

## A concrete walk-through

You add a quality burn to the weekly SLO review. A week of 100% uptime and 80% citations is red. Prompt work gets the error budget, not a new banner.

## What I would measure

Routes with all three SLOs; pages that were vibe-only; quality sample rate.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on Define **SLOs for availability, latency, and quality** — not only uptime. An LLM is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) SLOs: availability, latency, quality; 2) Uptime alone is not enough; 3) Page on error rate and p95 (and quality burns); 4) Quality needs a sample and a calibrated judge or humans; 5) Per-route SLOs, not one blob. The spoken close stays the same: I set SLOs on availability, p95, and quality, and I page on error rate and p95 — not on vibe or GPU utilisation. 100% uptime with wrong answers is a miss.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

Uptime alone is not enough.
Page on error rate and p95 (and quality burns).
Quality needs a sample and a calibrated judge or humans.
Per-route SLOs, not one blob.
Error budgets include quality.

questions.a: Latency tails and quality. The feature can be up and unusable or wrong.

questions.a: Error rate and p95 (and a quality burn if you can compute it fast). Not vibe, not GPU busy.

questions.a: A sampled online eval, a calibrated judge, plus a golden replay on each release.

questions.q: Why per-route SLOs?
questions.a: FAQ and refunds have different p95 and quality floors. A blend hides the scary one.

questions.q: What is a useful availability definition?
questions.a: Share of requests that received the intended useful path (including a designed degrade), not merely HTTP 200 from a spinner.

questions.q: What is the default degrade when generation is down?

3. **No schema on arrows.**

## A concrete walk-through

You redraw a hairball into a line plus three workers. p95 becomes explainable. The agent loop is one optional box, not the whole page.

The spoken close stays the same: I draw the end-to-end flow: retrieve, generate, validate, stream on the user path; ingest, embed, and eval on queues. If I cannot draw it, I do not understand the orchestration yet.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.

User path is short and sync or streamed.
Ingest and eval are async.
Arrows have schemas.

questions.q: Which steps belong on the user request thread?
questions.a: Retrieve (maybe cached), assemble, generate, validate, render. Not ingest, not full eval, not a 10-minute research loop.

questions.a: Serving p95 does not wait on parse/embed, and a bad doc dies in a DLQ instead of a user request.

questions.a: Independent evolution, validation, and the ability to swap a box.

questions.a: Queue it, return a job id, stream or notify later. Sync HTTP cannot hold that.

questions.a: One trace id that visits the same boxes. If a box is on the diagram but not in traces, it is fiction.

deterministic-vs-model-delegated-decisio.explain:
## What it is

Decide **which decisions are deterministic code** and which you **delegate to the model**. Deterministic: authZ, amounts, routing tables, schema checks, ACL, timeouts, 'is this a refund route'. Delegated: phrasing, which of three already-allowed docs to quote, whether a question is in scope *as a signal*. 

**Model proposes, code disposes** is the slogan. If you can write the rule in ten lines, do not spend a token on it. Ten sequential 95% model decisions are ~60% end-to-end — that is why you do not delegate the spine.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the judgement interviewers want. On the job it is how you keep a pipeline reliable.

## How it works + one small example

List decisions. Tick D or M. Refund limit D; tone M; retrieve filter D; which paragraph to quote M (with a grounding check D). If a D is implemented as a prompt, move it.

## Failure modes

1. **AuthZ in the prompt.**

2. **A chain of seven model calls** that could be a flowchart.

3. **Treating a classifier as D** without measuring it.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I put deterministic decisions in code — authZ, limits, ACL, schema — and I let the model propose phrasing and selection inside those fences. Model proposes, code disposes. I will not spend tokens on a ten-line rule.

## A concrete walk-through

You highlight seven prompt rules and move four into code. The remaining three are tone. Reliability stops depending on a wording.

## What I would measure

D decisions still in prompts; length of model-delegated chains; 0.95^n stories in reviews.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for Decide **which decisions are deterministic code** and which you **delegate to th and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) D versus M is an explicit list; 2) AuthZ, amounts, ACL, schema are D; 3) Phrasing and selection can be M inside fences; 4) Model proposes, code disposes; 5) A chain of 95% steps is a reliability hole. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I put deterministic decisions in code — authZ, limits, ACL, schema — and I let the model propose phrasing and selection inside those fences. Model proposes, code disposes. I will not spend tokens on a ten-line rule.

## What it is

Vercel-style request limits and user patience both cap sync. A 8-minute job on the request thread is a bug. Approvals make a workflow long-running even if each model call is fast.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Table: FAQ sync+stream; embed nightly queue; research job object with steps and a worker; approval wait is a state machine, not an open HTTP connection.

component-boundaries.explain:
## What it is

**Clear component boundaries** so you can **change, evaluate, and scale** parts independently. Retriever, assembler, model client, validator, tool executor, cache, ingest — each has an interface and a test. You can swap the embedding model without rewriting the executor. You can scale ingest workers without scaling the chat replicas.

Boundaries are schemas and owners, not folders. If changing a prompt requires a retriever rewrite, the boundary is a fiction.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how a system lives more than a quarter. Interviewers ask how you would swap a vendor.

## How it works + one small example

Interfaces: `Retriever.retrieve(ctx, q) -> Hits`; `Assembler.build(hits, rules) -> Prompt`; `Model.complete(prompt) -> Tokens`; `Validator.check(out)`. Each has a golden test. The gateway owns `Model`. Product owns `Assembler` rules.

## Failure modes

1. **A god class 'Agent'.**

2. **Shared mutable prompt string** everyone concatenates.

3. **Scaling the whole pod** because ingest is heavy.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I draw component boundaries — retrieve, assemble, model, validate, execute, ingest — with schemas and owners so I can swap, eval, and scale them independently. A god-class agent is not a boundary.

## A concrete walk-through

You split a 2k-line agent into five packages with contracts. The vendor swap is a 40-line adapter. Ingest gets its own deploy.

## What I would measure

Vendor SDKs imported outside the gateway; chat and ingest sharing HPA; contract tests per box.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on **Clear component boundaries** so you can **change, evaluate, and scale** parts , I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Interfaces and owners, not just folders; 2) Swap a vendor without rewriting the executor; 3) Scale ingest apart from chat; 4) Each box has a golden test; 5) A shared mutable prompt is a missing boundary. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: I draw component boundaries — retrieve, assemble, model, validate, execute, ingest — with schemas and owners so I can swap, eval, and scale them independently. A god-class agent is not a boundary.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.

Swap a vendor without rewriting the executor.
Scale ingest apart from chat.
Each box has a golden test.
A shared mutable prompt is a missing boundary.
A god-class agent will not age well.

questions.a: It is bursty and CPU/IO heavy. Chat wants reserved low-latency replicas. One pod size will hurt one of them.

what-to-monitor.explain:
## What it is

Monitor **quality, latency, cost, errors, retrieval behaviour, tool usage, and model/provider performance** — not only HTTP 200. Quality: sample scores, citation rate, thumbs. Latency: TTFT and p95 per route. Cost: $ per success and per feature. Errors: 5xx, schema fail, designed refuse. Retrieval: hit count, empty rate, forbidden-id canaries. Tools: count, deny, approve. Provider: error rate, model_id mix, fallback share.

A dashboard with seven panels is the design. A single green uptime is not.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Uptime-only monitoring is how wrong answers ship silently. Interviewers ask what is on the board.

## How it works + one small example

One board per product, seven rows. Alerting from M9.6 on the fast ones. Weekly read on quality and retrieval slices. When a model_id mix shifts, you already have the panel.

## Failure modes

1. **Uptime only.**

2. **Quality with no sample.**

3. **Cost as a monthly invoice** with no route tag.

4. **Retrieval with no empty-rate.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I monitor quality, latency, cost, errors, retrieval, tools, and providers — per route. Uptime alone is how silent wrongness ships. The board has seven panels, not one green dot.

## A concrete walk-through

You add empty-retrieve and model_id mix. A week later you see a fallback spike and a citation dip on the same hours. That is a wired board.

## What I would measure

Panels present; routes missing quality; invoices that cannot split by feature.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for Monitor **quality, latency, cost, errors, retrieval behaviour, tool usage, and m and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Seven families: quality, latency, cost, errors, retrieval, tools, provider; 2) Per route, not one blob; 3) Empty-retrieve and forbidden-id are retrieval panels; 4) Cost is $ per success, tagged; 5) Provider mix and fallback share are first-class. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I monitor quality, latency, cost, errors, retrieval, tools, and providers — per route. Uptime alone is how silent wrongness ships. The board has seven panels, not one green dot.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.

explicit-implicit-feedback.explain:
## What it is

Capture **explicit** feedback (thumbs, ratings, 'report wrong') and **useful implicit** signals (edits, regenerates, abandoned answers, copy-paste, time-to-next-message, escalation to a human). Explicit is sparse and biased. Implicit is plentiful and noisy. Together they label production.

Implicit is not surveillance theatre: pick signals that mean something for this product. A regenerate after 2 s is a different label than a long copy-paste.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you get labels without waiting for thumbs. Interviewers ask for an implicit example.

## How it works + one small example

Schema: `signal, weight, case_id`. Thumbs ±1. Regenerate within 5 s + negative. Edit of the answer + strong negative on the span. Escalation + negative on resolution. Weekly, humans review a sample of implicit labels to calibrate.

## Failure modes

1. **Thumbs only.**

2. **Every click is a label** with no calibration.

3. **Implicit that includes PII** you should not store.

4. **Treating no-thumb as positive.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I capture thumbs and implicit signals — edits, regenerates, abandons, escalations — and I calibrate them. No-thumb is not a win, and not every click is a label.

## A concrete walk-through

You add regenerate-within-5s as a case source. Calibration shows it is 70% true-negative. You use it to mine, not to auto-grade.

## What I would measure

Explicit rate; implicit-to-case rate; calibration precision of each signal.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on Capture **explicit** feedback (thumbs, ratings, 'report wrong') and **useful imp, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Explicit is sparse; implicit is plentiful and noisy; 2) Edits, regenerates, abandons, escalations are labels; 3) Calibrate implicit on a human sample; 4) No-thumb is not positive; 5) Do not store implicit that is just more PII. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: I capture thumbs and implicit signals — edits, regenerates, abandons, escalations — and I calibrate them. No-thumb is not a win, and not every click is a label.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.

Edits, regenerates, abandons, escalations are labels.
Calibrate implicit on a human sample.
No-thumb is not positive.
Do not store implicit that is just more PII.
Signal and weight live on the case.

questions.a: User regenerates within a few seconds, edits the answer, abandons, or escalates to a human. Treat as a noisy negative and calibrate.

questions.a: Most users never click. You would label the world good and hide failures.

questions.q: How do you keep implicit from being junk?
questions.a: A small set of signals, weights, and a weekly human calibration sample.

questions.a: Escalation after the bot answered, or an agent rewriting the draft heavily.

failures-become-evaluation-cases.explain:
## What it is

**Every production failure and useful feedback row becomes a case** in the eval set — with a de-duplication and privacy pass. The loop is: fail → label → add → run on the next build → prevent regression. A single failing case that you fix by editing the prompt **must** enter the suite or the next model bump will bring it back.

Do not add raw PII. Redact. Do not add 400 near-duplicates; cluster.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the immune system. Interviewers ask what you do after a one-off prompt fix.

## How it works + one small example

Button on the trace: 'add to eval'. Pipeline redacts, assigns an id, and opens a PR or writes to the store. Nightly run includes it. The prompt PR that 'fixed' it is blocked until the case is green.

## Failure modes

1. **Fix and forget.**

2. **Adding raw tickets** to a public repo.

3. **A 10,000-case pile** of duplicates that nobody trusts.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Failures become evaluation cases. A prompt-only fix without a case is not done. I redact, I de-dupe, and I block the fix PR until the case is in the suite.

## A concrete walk-through

IR-88 becomes `eval/ir88.json` in the same PR as the prompt fix. CI is red until both land. A month later a model bump fails ir88; you keep the prompt.

## What I would measure

Incidents without a case; prompt PRs without a new case; PII in the suite.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for **Every production failure and useful feedback row becomes a case** in the eval  and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Fail → label → add → run → no regression; 2) Prompt fixes require a case; 3) Redact PII; do not dump tickets into git; 4) De-dupe near-copies; 5) A button on the trace beats a cultural hope. The sentence I can say under pressure is: Failures become evaluation cases. A prompt-only fix without a case is not done. I redact, I de-dupe, and I block the fix PR until the case is in the suite.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.
## A note on residual risk

I treat leftover risk on **every production failure and useful feedback row becomes a case** in the eval  as something I can name, not as a vibe. If a control is probabilistic I say the residual attack or error rate. If a number is missing I write the smallest measurement that would change my mind. I would rather ship a smaller surface with a written residual than a larger one I cannot explain. The owner of that residual is a person, and the review date is on a calendar.

questions.a: Add a redacted case to the suite and prove the new prompt passes it. Otherwise the next bump regresses.

versioning-for-traceable-regressions.explain:
## What it is

**Version models, prompts, retrieval configs, and application changes** so a regression can be attributed. Every answer carries `model_id, prompt_id, retriever_id, app_sha`. Evals run against a build. When quality drops on Tuesday, you diff those four, not the org chart.

Versioning is not 'v2' in a wiki. It is an id in the trace and a pin in the gateway.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you debug a quality regression in an hour instead of a week. Interviewers ask how you attribute.

## How it works + one small example

Gateway pins `model_id`. Prompt store has immutable ids. Retriever config is a hash of index snapshot + params. App SHA from deploy. The eval report prints all four. Rollbacks are a pin revert.

## Failure modes

1. **`latest` everywhere.**

2. **Prompt in code with no id.**

3. **Index rebuilt with no snapshot id.**

4. **A quality drop with no join key.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I version models, prompts, retrieval configs, and app SHAs on every answer so a regression is a diff, not a mystery. Pins beat `latest`. Rollback is a pin revert.

## A concrete walk-through

Tuesday dips. You join traces: `retriever_id` changed, model did not. You revert the pin. That is versioning as operations.

## What I would measure

Answers missing a version; uses of latest; time-to-attribute a dip.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on **Version models, prompts, retrieval configs, and application changes** so a reg is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Four ids: model, prompt, retriever, app; 2) They ride on every trace and eval report; 3) Pins, not latest; 4) Rollback is reverting a pin; 5) Index rebuilds get a snapshot id. The spoken close stays the same: I version models, prompts, retrieval configs, and app SHAs on every answer so a regression is a diff, not a mystery. Pins beat `latest`. Rollback is a pin revert.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.
## A note on residual risk

I treat leftover risk on **version models, prompts, retrieval configs, and application changes** so a reg as something I can name, not as a vibe. If a control is probabilistic I say the residual attack or error rate. If a number is missing I write the smallest measurement that would change my mind. I would rather ship a smaller surface with a written residual than a larger one I cannot explain. The owner of that residual is a person, and the review date is on a calendar.
keyPoints: Four ids: model, prompt, retriever, app.
They ride on every trace and eval report.
Pins, not latest.
Rollback is reverting a pin.
Index rebuilds get a snapshot id.
Attribution is a join, not a meeting.

questions.a: Pin and log model, prompt, retriever, and app versions so you can diff Tuesday against Monday.

questions.q: Best rollout method for a new retrieval configuration?
questions.a: A versioned pin, a canary or percentage, and a compare on the same eval — not an unversioned rebuild of prod.

questions.q: Prompt lives as a string in a handler. What is missing?
questions.a: An immutable id and a store. You cannot say which wording served.

questions.q: How do you rollback a bad model?
questions.a: Revert the gateway pin to the last green snapshot, after the eval says so.

questions.q: Why is `latest` a versioning bug?
questions.a: The world can change on a Thursday without a deploy or an eval.

whiteboard-and-defend-the-choices.explain:
## What it is

A capstone design is a **whiteboard you can defend**: several systems end-to-end, each with requirements, a baseline, a pick, trade-offs, evals, and a cut list. Defending means you can say why not the alternatives, what you would drop, and which number would prove you wrong. Pretty boxes without a defence are a poster.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the Level 9 exam. Interviewers will switch products mid-board. On the job it is how staff reviews land.

## How it works + one small example

Practise three: support copilot, coding assistant, deep research. Same agenda (M9.1), different binding constraints. When they change the latency budget, you keep the skeleton and swap the pick.

## Failure modes

1. **One memorised diagram** for every product.
2. **No why-not.**
3. **No number that would prove you wrong.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I whiteboard several systems and defend each pick: requirements, options, trade-offs, eval, and a cut list. If I cannot say why not the alternatives, I have a poster, not a design.

## A concrete walk-through

You run a 30-minute timer on each product once a week. By the interview you can defend, not recite.

## What I would measure

## What it is

A **deep research agent** is designed around **search and retrieval**, **planning**, **parallel tool calls**, **context management**, **long-running execution**, **citations**, and **cost budgets and failure recovery**. The user wants a sourced report, not a chatty guess. Time is minutes; money is dollars; the binding risks are wander, cost, and unsourced claims.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Third capstone product. Interviewers expect this list and a budget.

## How it works + one small example

5 minutes: requirements (minutes, $, cite-all-claims); areas; pick (capped loop, not a 12-agent org chart); eval (citation precision, task success); cut (fewer sources, smaller model, shorter budget).

## Failure modes

1. **No budget.**
2. **No citations.**
3. **A dozen agents** with no owner.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Deep research is search, plan, parallel tools, context, a long job, citations, and a budget with recovery. I cap the loop, I cite every claim, and I do not ship a dozen unmanaged agents.

## A concrete walk-through

You name the seven, circle budget and cites, and refuse the org chart. That is the 5-minute talk.

## What I would measure

Areas named; designs with no budget or no cites.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on A **deep research agent** is designed around **search and retrieval**, **plannin, I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Seven areas as listed; 2) Minutes and dollars, not 3 s; 3) Cite-all-claims is a requirement; 4) Capped loop over a 12-agent org chart; 5) Cut list: sources, model, budget. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: Deep research is search, plan, parallel tools, context, a long job, citations, and a budget with recovery. I cap the loop, I cite every claim, and I do not ship a dozen unmanaged agents.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.
keyPoints: Seven areas as listed.
Minutes and dollars, not 3 s.
Cite-all-claims is a requirement.
Capped loop over a 12-agent org chart.
Cut list: sources, model, budget.
Wander and cost are the risks.

questions.q: What are the main design areas for a deep research agent?
questions.a: Search/retrieval, planning, parallel tools, context management, long-running execution, citations, cost budgets and failure recovery.

questions.q: You have 5 minutes to present the deep research agent. How do you spend them?
questions.a: Requirements (time, $, cite-all), the areas, a capped loop, eval, and a cut list. Not a 12-agent slide.

questions.q: What binds this product versus support?
questions.a: Minutes and dollars, not 3 s p95. Citations and budget dominate.

questions.q: Why not twelve agents?
questions.a: Ownership, eval, and cost. A capped loop with parallel tools is enough until an eval slice says otherwise.

questions.q: What is the cut if the deadline moved a week left?
questions.a: Fewer sources, smaller model, shorter budget — keep citations and the job record.

search-retrieval.explain:
## What it is

Research search is **web + optional private index**, with a **quarantined reader** (Level 8) so pages cannot steal tools. Retrieve, reread, store raw pages **outside** the prompt, and pull quotes in. Dedup sources. Do not fetch 5,000 URLs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

First research area. Hidden HTML is back.

## How it works + one small example

Search API → url allow-list → reader strips hidden text → store raw → retrieve quotes into the window. Cap fetches per host and total.

## Failure modes

1. **Raw HTML in the privileged prompt.**
2. **No fetch cap.**
3. **No store of raw pages**, so you cannot cite later.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I search, I read in a quarantine, I store raw pages outside the prompt, and I pull quotes in. Hidden HTML never meets the send tool, and I cap fetches.

## A concrete walk-through

You split reader and planner. A planted comment no longer reaches the report loop.

## What I would measure

Fetches per run; hidden-text in planner context; uncapped hosts.

## Interview follow-up

A good fork on Research search is **web + optional private index**, with a **quarantined reader is: what would convince me I was wrong by Friday. I want a metric, a fixture, or a trace — not a vibe. I will defend these points if interrupted: 1) Web + private index; 2) Quarantined reader; 3) Raw pages stored out of prompt; 4) Quotes in, not whole pages; 5) Fetch caps per host and total. The spoken close stays the same: I search, I read in a quarantine, I store raw pages outside the prompt, and I pull quotes in. Hidden HTML never meets the send tool, and I cap fetches.

If they ask for tools, I name a vendor doc only after the design. Tools change; the boundary does not. If they ask for a war story, I give one number and one change, then offer to go deeper.

## How this fails in a real review

Teams skip this when a demo is due. The skip shows up later as an incident, a surprise bill, or a questionnaire they cannot answer. I write the failure modes into the runbook so the next on-call does not rediscover them. I also refuse a change that cannot be tested, versioned, and rolled back.

## What I would do on Monday

I would schedule a one-hour review with the sketch or the eval set on the table, file the missing test, and add the metric to the weekly dashboard. If leadership wants a slide, the slide is k/n or p95 or cost per successful task — the same number I would use in the interview.
## A note on residual risk

I treat leftover risk on research search is **web + optional private index**, with a **quarantined reader as something I can name, not as a vibe. If a control is probabilistic I say the residual attack or error rate. If a number is missing I write the smallest measurement that would change my mind. I would rather ship a smaller surface with a written residual than a larger one I cannot explain. The owner of that residual is a person, and the review date is on a calendar.
## What I would ask next

Three questions I keep next to research search is **web + optional private index**, with a **quarantined reader: who is harmed if this is wrong, how quickly we would notice, and what we would stop doing. If I cannot answer those in a sentence each, the design is not ready for a whiteboard. I write the answers on the diagram so the interview is about the system, not my memory.

Quarantined reader.
Raw pages stored out of prompt.
Quotes in, not whole pages.
Fetch caps per host and total.
Dedup sources.

questions.q: Why store raw fetched pages outside the prompt?
questions.a: So you can cite, reread, and not blow the window — and so the privileged loop does not sit on raw HTML.

questions.q: What does the reader drop?
questions.a: Scripts, comments, hidden nodes — Level 8's HTML lesson.

questions.q: How do you stop a 5,000-URL wander?
questions.a: Total and per-host caps, duplicate URL block, dollar budget.

questions.q: Can the privileged planner fetch arbitrary URLs?
questions.a: No. It asks a reader worker that returns structured quotes.

questions.q: What is dedup for?
questions.a: The same wire story on ten domains should be one source cluster.

## What it is

A research **plan** is a short, revisable outline: questions, sources to try, a done definition. The model may write it; the harness **stores** it and checks it against the budget. Re-plan when a branch dies. Do not re-plan every token. A plan that is only in the rolling chat will mutate into a different task (goal drift).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers ask how you avoid wander.

## How it works + one small example

Object: `Plan{questions[], done_when, budget}`. Worker updates checkboxes. Drift detector: new questions must map to the original user ask or get user confirm.

## Failure modes

1. **Plan only in chat.**
2. **Re-plan every step.**
3. **No done definition.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep a stored plan with a done definition and a budget, and I treat goal drift as a bug. The plan is not only in the chat, and I do not re-plan every token.

## A concrete walk-through

You persist the plan. A 15-minute run still answers the original three questions.

## What I would measure

Drift events; plans only in chat; runs without done-when.

requirements-architecture-trade-offs.explain:
## What it is

For each capstone case, walk **requirements → baseline → architecture → bottlenecks → failure modes → scaling → trade-offs**. That is the long form of the 30-minute agenda. Support, coding, and research each get this walk. The trade-offs are the triangle plus complexity: e.g. research quality vs $ vs wander; coding complete vs agent vs sandbox friction.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the meta-item that ties the three products to M9.1.

## How it works + one small example

One page per product with those seven headings. Practise saying the trade-offs in two sentences each.

## Failure modes

1. **Jumping to architecture.**
2. **No bottlenecks.**
3. **No scaling story** (what breaks at 10×).

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I walk requirements, baseline, architecture, bottlenecks, failures, scaling, and trade-offs for each case. That is how I evaluate a research agent — or a copilot — before launch, and how I talk about trade-offs without a slogan.

## A concrete walk-through

You write three one-pagers with the seven headings. The interview is those pages spoken.

## What I would measure

Products without a 10× sentence; walks that skip baseline.

## Interview follow-up

When the interviewer changes the constraints — half the latency budget, a new region, a hostile document, a cheaper model — I keep the same skeleton for For each capstone case, walk **requirements → baseline → architecture → bottlene and swap the binding constraint. The skeleton is: 1) Seven headings per product; 2) Baseline before architecture; 3) Name bottlenecks and 10× breaks; 4) Trade-offs are the triangle plus complexity; 5) Do not jump to boxes. The sentence I can say under pressure is: I walk requirements, baseline, architecture, bottlenecks, failures, scaling, and trade-offs for each case. That is how I evaluate a research agent — or a copilot — before launch, and how I talk about trade-offs without a slogan.

I do not restart from a blank architecture. That is what junior answers do. I show what I would drop first and what I would never drop.

## How this fails in a real review

This topic dies when it lives only in a prompt or a wiki page. Prompts regress on the next model bump; wiki pages do not run in CI. I put the control in code and the proof in a test. I also watch for correlated layers that look like depth and fail together.

## What I would do on Monday

I would pair with the owner of the executor, the retriever, or the gateway — whichever box this topic touches — and add the smallest check that would have caught last quarter's near-miss. Then I would re-run the relevant suite or eval and write the delta in the release notes.
## A note on residual risk

I treat leftover risk on for each capstone case, walk **requirements → baseline → architecture → bottlene as something I can name, not as a vibe. If a control is probabilistic I say the residual attack or error rate. If a number is missing I write the smallest measurement that would change my mind. I would rather ship a smaller surface with a written residual than a larger one I cannot explain. The owner of that residual is a person, and the review date is on a calendar.

questions.q: State three trade-offs in a deep research agent design and how you resolve them.
questions.a: Quality vs $ (budget + small-first search); completeness vs latency (caps and partials); wander vs coverage (stored plan). Resolve with numbers, not vibes.

questions.q: How would you evaluate the research agent before launch?
questions.a: A labelled set of research tasks with citation precision, task success, $ and minutes per task, and a wander/drift rate.

questions.q: What heading do people skip?
questions.a: Bottlenecks and 10× scaling — what breaks when traffic or corpus grows.

questions.q: Where does the baseline sit in the walk?
questions.a: Right after requirements, before the fancy architecture.

questions.q: Give a 10× break for support RAG.
questions.a: The index or the provider QPS; p95 and $ per ticket blow up if you did not cache and route.

the-one-pager-a-staff-engineer-would-sig.explain:
## What it is

A staff one-pager is **requirements, diagram, risks, eval, cost, and rollback** — one page, not a novel. Requirements: users, SLOs, data class. Diagram: the boxes you will actually ship. Risks: the one path (security) and the one bottleneck. Eval: n, metric, threshold. Cost: $ per job. Rollback: which pin you revert. If a staff engineer would not sign it, it is not done.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the missing close of the capstone. Interviewers will ask what you would send to a VP.

## How it works + one small example

Template with those six sections, versioned with the release. No vendor poetry. A link to the system card and the threat sketch.

## Failure modes

1. **A 20-page doc** nobody reads.
2. **No rollback.**
3. **No $.**
4. **A diagram of the wishlist.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write a one-pager a staff engineer would sign: requirements, the real diagram, risks, eval, cost, and rollback. If rollback or $ is missing, it is not signable.

## A concrete walk-through

You replace a 20-pager with six sections. The VP signs. The wishlist moves to an appendix.

## What I would measure

One-pagers missing rollback or $; novels without a diagram of the ship.

## Interview follow-up

If they push on A staff one pager is **requirements, diagram, risks, eval, cost, and rollback** , I do not invent a second framework. I pick one control, one number, and the residual risk. The points I will not drop: 1) Six sections: reqs, diagram, risks, eval, cost, rollback; 2) The diagram is the ship, not the wishlist; 3) Rollback is a pin; 4) Cost is $ per job; 5) Link the card and the threat sketch. If they only have thirty seconds left I repeat the line and stop: I write a one-pager a staff engineer would sign: requirements, the real diagram, risks, eval, cost, and rollback. If rollback or $ is missing, it is not signable.

A common trap is answering a different question — a model-vendor anecdote, a tool name, a blog slogan. I steer back to the boundary or the metric. If they ask what I would cut with a week less, I cut the probabilistic layer first and keep the deterministic one.

## How this fails in a real review

The cheap objection is that this is overkill for a prototype. A prototype can be smaller, but the constraint still belongs in writing so we do not promote the prototype unchanged. Another objection is that the next model will make the problem go away. A better model does not remove a missing ACL, a shared admin token, an unmeasured p95, or a cache key without a tenant. I ask what still has to be true if the model is perfect.

## What I would do on Monday

I would add one test or one dashboard panel that makes this topic visible, name an owner in the design doc, and put the thirty-second line at the top of the PR. If I cannot name the owner and the metric, I do not understand the work yet. I would rather ship a smaller capability with a measured residual than a demo that fails the first red team or the first traffic spike.
keyPoints: Six sections: reqs, diagram, risks, eval, cost, rollback.
The diagram is the ship, not the wishlist.
Rollback is a pin.
Cost is $ per job.
Link the card and the threat sketch.
A novel is not a one-pager.

questions.q: What six sections are on the staff one-pager?
questions.a: Requirements, diagram, risks, eval, cost, and rollback.

questions.q: What makes it 'signable'?
questions.a: Real SLOs, a shippable diagram, a falsifying eval, a dollar number, and a rollback pin — no wishlist poetry.

questions.q: A 20-page design has no rollback. Sign?
questions.a: No. Ask for the pin you revert on Tuesday.

questions.q: Where does the threat sketch live?
questions.a: Linked from risks, one path highlighted.

questions.q: What cost number belongs here?
questions.a: $ per successful job (ticket, complete, research report), not a vague GPU hope.

Writing the cut list is how you prove you know what is load-bearing.

## Failure modes

1. **Cutting ACL or sandbox** to 'ship'.
2. **No cut list**, so they cut at random under pressure.
3. **Cutting the eval.**

If the deadline moved a week left I cut non-load-bearing quality extras — rerankers, extra agents, extra sources — and I keep ACL, sandbox, cites, budget, eval, and the human path. The cut list is written before I need it.

You write nine bullets (three products). In the interview you only need 15 seconds. That is the last item.

questions.q: What would you drop if the deadline moved a week left — support?
questions.a: Reranker and any agent loop. Keep retrieve-and-generate, ACL, cites, escalate, eval.

questions.q: What do you never cut?
questions.a: Security boundaries (ACL, sandbox), eval, and the human path. Those are load-bearing.

questions.q: Why write the list before you need it?
questions.a: Under deadline people cut randomly. The list is the defence of what stays.

questions.q: Research cut list?
questions.a: Fewer sources, smaller model, shorter budget. Keep cites, job record, and the budget mechanism.

questions.q: A PM wants to cut the eval to ship. Your line?
questions.a: Then we cannot know if we shipped. The eval stays; we cut a feature instead.
